Chapter 6 · Geography · Contemporary India II

Manufacturing Industries

Manufacturing is the backbone of development: it modernises agriculture, creates jobs, earns foreign exchange and makes a country prosperous. This chapter classifies India’s industries, explains where each one located itself and why, and ends with industrial pollution and how NTPC shows the way.

Chapter Overview

What this chapter is about, at a glance

Production of goods in large quantities after processing from raw materials to more valuable products is called manufacturing. Paper is manufactured from wood, sugar from sugarcane, iron and steel from iron ore and aluminium from bauxite. People employed in the secondary activities manufacture the primary materials into finished goods — workers in steel factories, car plants, breweries, textile industries and bakeries.

The chapter argues that the economic strength of a country is measured by the development of manufacturing industries. Manufacturing modernises agriculture, reduces dependence on agricultural income by providing jobs in secondary and tertiary sectors, helps eradicate unemployment and poverty, brings down regional disparities, and expands trade and commerce, earning foreign exchange.

It then classifies industries on five bases — source of raw material, main role, capital investment, ownership, and bulk and weight — and describes the agro-based industries (cotton textiles, jute, sugar) and mineral-based industries (iron and steel, aluminium smelting, chemicals, fertiliser, cement, automobile, IT and electronics).

The final section deals with industrial pollution — air, water, land and noise — and the steps to control environmental degradation, including the three phases of effluent treatment and the example of NTPC.

Manufacturing

Production of goods in large quantities after processing raw materials into more valuable products; it belongs to the secondary sector.

Textile industry

The only industry in the country that is self-reliant and complete in the value chain, from raw material to the highest value added products.

Firsts

First successful textile mill in Mumbai in 1854; first jute mill near Kolkata at Rishra in 1855; first cement plant in Chennai in 1904.

Iron and steel

A basic as well as heavy industry; iron ore, coking coal and limestone are needed in the ratio of approximately 4:2:1.

Aluminium

4 to 6 tonnes of bauxite give 2 tonnes of alumina, which give 1 tonne of aluminium.

Sugar

India is second in the world in sugar production but first in gur and khandsari; 60 per cent of mills are in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

Fertiliser

Potash (K) is entirely imported — India has no commercially usable reserves.

Pollution

Industries cause air, water, land and noise pollution; effluent treatment has primary, secondary and tertiary phases.

What is Manufacturing?
NCERT definition

Production of goods in large quantities after processing from raw materials to more valuable products is called manufacturing.

Do you know that paper is manufactured from wood, sugar from sugarcane, iron and steel from iron ore and aluminium from bauxite? Do you also know that some types of clothes are manufactured from yarn, which itself is an industrial product?

People employed in the secondary activities manufacture the primary materials into finished goods. The workers employed in steel factories, car plants, breweries, textile industries and bakeries fall into this category. Some people are employed in providing services. In this chapter we are mainly concerned with manufacturing industries, which fall in the secondary sector.

The economic strength of a country is measured by the development of manufacturing industries.

Chapter story

On the occasion of Diwali, Harish went to a market with his parents. They purchased shoes and clothes for him. His mother purchased utensils, sugar, tea and diyas (earthen lamps). Harish observed that the shops in the market were flooded with items for sale. He wondered how so many items could be made in such large quantities. His father explained that shoes, clothes, sugar etc. are manufactured by machines in large industries, some utensils are manufactured in small industries, while items like diyas are made by individual artisans in household industry.

Do it yourself

Do you have some ideas about these industries?

Importance of Manufacturing

The manufacturing sector is considered the backbone of development in general and economic development in particular, mainly because:

  • Manufacturing industries not only help in modernising agriculture, which forms the backbone of our economy, they also reduce the heavy dependence of people on agricultural income by providing them jobs in secondary and tertiary sectors.
  • Industrial development is a precondition for eradication of unemployment and poverty from our country. This was the main philosophy behind public sector industries and joint sector ventures in India. It was also aimed at bringing down regional disparities by establishing industries in tribal and backward areas.
  • Export of manufactured goods expands trade and commerce, and brings in much needed foreign exchange.
  • Countries that transform their raw materials into a wide variety of finished goods of higher value are prosperous.

India’s prosperity lies in increasing and diversifying its manufacturing industries as quickly as possible.

Agriculture and industry are not exclusive of each other. They move hand in hand. For instance, the agro-industries in India have given a major boost to agriculture by raising its productivity. They depend on the latter for raw materials and sell their products such as irrigation pumps, fertilisers, insecticides, pesticides, plastic and PVC pipes, machines and tools, etc. to the farmers. Thus the development and competitiveness of the manufacturing industry has not only assisted agriculturists in increasing their production but also made the production processes very efficient.

In the present-day world of globalisation, our industry needs to be more efficient and competitive. Self-sufficiency alone is not enough. Our manufactured goods must be at par in quality with those in the international market. Only then will we be able to compete in the international market.

Classification of Industries

List the various manufactured products you use in your daily life — transistors, electric bulbs, vegetable oil, cement, glassware, petrol, matches, scooters, automobiles, medicines and so on. If we classify the various industries based on a particular criterion, we would be able to understand their manufacturing better. Industries may be classified as follows.

Classification of industries
BasisTypeExamples / meaning
Source of raw materialAgro-basedCotton, woollen, jute, silk textile, rubber and sugar, tea, coffee, edible oil
Source of raw materialMineral-basedIron and steel, cement, aluminium, machine tools, petrochemicals

Main roleConsumer industriesProduce goods for direct use by consumers — sugar, toothpaste, paper, sewing machines, fans
Capital investmentSmall scale industryDefined with reference to the maximum investment allowed on the assets of a unit; at present the maximum investment allowed is rupees one crore
OwnershipPublic sectorOwned and operated by government agencies — BHEL, SAIL
OwnershipPrivate sectorOwned and operated by individuals or a group of individuals — TISCO, Bajaj Auto Ltd., Dabur Industries

Activity

Classify the following into two groups on the basis of bulk and weight of raw material and finished goods: (i) Oil (ii) Knitting needles (iii) Brassware (iv) Fuse wires (v) Watches (vi) Sewing machines (vii) Shipbuilding (viii) Electric bulbs (ix) Paint brushes (x) Automobiles.

Teacher explanation

Suggested grouping: Heavy industries — oil, shipbuilding, automobiles, sewing machines, brassware. Light industries — knitting needles, fuse wires, watches, electric bulbs, paint brushes. The test is the bulk and weight of both the raw material and the finished product.

Agro-based Industries: Textiles, Jute and Sugar

Cotton, jute, silk and woollen textiles, sugar and edible oil, etc., industries are based on agricultural raw materials.

Textile industry

The textile industry occupies a unique position in the Indian economy, because it contributes significantly to industrial production, employment generation and foreign exchange earnings. It is the only industry in the country which is self-reliant and complete in the value chain, i.e. from raw material to the highest value added products.

Cotton textiles

In ancient India, cotton textiles were produced with hand spinning and handloom weaving techniques. After the 18th century, power-looms came into use. Our traditional industries suffered a setback during the colonial period because they could not compete with the mill-made cloth from England.

  • The first successful textile mill was established in Mumbai in 1854.
  • The two World Wars were fought in Europe; India was a British colony. There was a demand for cloth in the United Kingdom, hence the British gave a boost to the development of the cotton textile industry.

In the early years, the cotton textile industry was concentrated in the cotton growing belt of Maharashtra and Gujarat. Availability of raw cotton, market, transport including accessible port facilities, labour, moist climate, etc., contributed towards its localisation.

This industry has close links with agriculture and provides a living to farmers, cotton boll pluckers and workers engaged in ginning, spinning, weaving, dyeing, designing, packaging, tailoring and sewing. The industry, by creating demand, supports many other industries such as chemicals and dyes, packaging materials and engineering works.

While spinning continues to be centralised in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu, weaving is highly decentralised to provide scope for incorporating traditional skills and designs of weaving in cotton, silk, zari and embroidery. India has world-class production in spinning, but weaving supplies low quality fabric as it cannot use much of the high quality yarn produced in the country. Weaving is done by handloom, powerloom and in mills. The handspun khadi provides large-scale employment to weavers in their homes as a cottage industry.

Do it yourself

Why did Mahatma Gandhi lay emphasis on spinning yarn and weaving khadi? Why is it important for our country to keep the mill sector loomage lower than power loom and handloom?

Jute textiles

India is the largest producer of raw jute and jute goods and stands at second place as an exporter after Bangladesh. Most of the mills are located in West Bengal, mainly along the banks of the Hugli river, in a narrow belt.

Factors responsible for their location in the Hugli basin are: proximity of the jute producing areas, inexpensive water transport, supported by a good network of railways, roadways and waterways to facilitate movement of raw material to the mills, abundant water for processing raw jute, cheap labour from West Bengal and adjoining states of Bihar, Odisha and Uttar Pradesh. Kolkata as a large urban centre provides banking, insurance and port facilities for export of jute goods.

The first jute mill was set up near Kolkata in 1855 at Rishra. After Partition in 1947, the jute mills remained in India but three-fourths of the jute producing area went to Bangladesh (erstwhile East Pakistan).

Sugar industry

India stands second as a world producer of sugar but occupies the first place in the production of gur and khandsari. The raw material used in this industry is bulky, and in haulage its sucrose content reduces. The mills are located in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Punjab, Haryana and Madhya Pradesh. Sixty per cent of mills are in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. This industry is seasonal in nature, so it is ideally suited to the cooperative sector.

In recent years there is a tendency for the mills to shift and concentrate in the southern and western states, especially in Maharashtra. This is because the cane produced here has a higher sucrose content. The cooler climate also ensures a longer crushing season. Moreover, the cooperatives are more successful in these states.

Do it yourself

Can you explain why the sugar industry is ideally suited to the cooperative sector?

Teacher explanation

Answer: because the industry is seasonal and the raw material — sugarcane — is bulky and loses sucrose after harvesting. Farmers must crush their cane quickly, so they pool resources in cooperatives, which share profits or losses proportionately. This is why the sugar industry in Maharashtra and the coir industry in Kerala are named as cooperative examples.

Mineral-based Industries: Iron and Steel

Industries that use minerals and metals as raw materials are called mineral-based industries.

The iron and steel industry is the basic industry, since all other industries — heavy, medium and light — depend on it for their machinery. Steel is needed to manufacture a variety of engineering goods, construction material, defence, medical, telephonic and scientific equipment, and a variety of consumer goods.

Production and consumption of steel is often regarded as the index of a country’s development. Iron and steel is a heavy industry because all the raw materials as well as finished goods are heavy and bulky, entailing heavy transportation costs. Iron ore, coking coal and limestone are required in the ratio of approximately 4:2:1. Some quantities of manganese are also required to harden the steel.

Where should steel plants be ideally located? Remember that the finished products also need an efficient transport network for distribution to markets and consumers.

The Chhotanagpur plateau region has the maximum concentration of iron and steel industries. It is largely because of the relative advantages this region has for the development of this industry. These include low cost of iron ore, high grade raw materials in proximity, cheap labour and vast growth potential in the home market.

Do it yourself

Make a list of all such goods made of steel that you can think of.

Hand spinning and handloom weaving give way to power-looms in cotton textiles.
Established in Mumbai.
Set up near Kolkata at Rishra.
Set up in Chennai; the industry expanded after Independence.
Jute mills remained in India but three-fourths of the jute producing area went to Bangladesh.
Aluminium Smelting

Aluminium smelting is the second most important metallurgical industry in India. It is light, resistant to corrosion, a good conductor of heat, malleable, and becomes strong when mixed with other metals. It is used to manufacture aircraft, utensils and wires. It has gained popularity as a substitute for steel, copper, zinc and lead in a number of industries.

Aluminium smelting plants in the country are located in Odisha, West Bengal, Kerala, Uttar Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu.

Bauxite, the raw material used in the smelters, is a very bulky, dark reddish coloured rock. Regular supply of electricity and an assured source of raw material at minimum cost are the two prime factors for the location of the industry.

The flow chart shows the process of manufacturing aluminium: bauxite from the quarry is transported by rail or ship to the aluminium refinery, where it is crushed and alumina dissolved out; bulk ore is shipped to the smelter site, where calcinated petroleum coke from a refinery and pitch from a colliery are added, with cryolite acting as a molten electrolyte, and electricity (18,600 kWh per tonne of ore) completes the smelting.

Chemical, Fertiliser and Cement Industries

Chemical industries

The chemical industry in India is fast growing and diversifying. It comprises both large and small scale manufacturing units. Rapid growth has been recorded in both inorganic and organic sectors.

Inorganic chemicals include sulphuric acid (used to manufacture fertilisers, synthetic fibres, plastics, adhesives, paints and dye-stuffs), nitric acid, alkalies, soda ash (used to make glass, soaps and detergents, paper) and caustic soda. These industries are widely spread over the country.

Organic chemicals include petrochemicals, which are used for manufacturing synthetic fibres, synthetic rubber, plastics, dye-stuffs, drugs and pharmaceuticals. Organic chemical plants are located near oil refineries or petrochemical plants.

The chemical industry is its own largest consumer. Basic chemicals undergo processing to further produce other chemicals that are used for industrial application, agriculture or directly for consumer markets.

Fertiliser industry

The fertiliser industry is centred around the production of nitrogenous fertilisers (mainly urea), phosphatic fertilisers and ammonium phosphate (DAP) and complex fertilisers, which have a combination of nitrogen (N), phosphate (P) and potash (K). The third, i.e. potash, is entirely imported, as the country does not have any reserves of commercially usable potash or potassium compounds in any form.

After the Green Revolution the industry expanded to several other parts of the country. Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Kerala contribute towards half of the fertiliser production. Other significant producers are Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Rajasthan, Bihar, Maharashtra, Assam, West Bengal, Goa, Delhi, Madhya Pradesh and Karnataka.

Cement industry

Cement is essential for construction activity such as building houses, factories, bridges, roads, airports, dams and other commercial establishments. This industry requires bulky and heavy raw materials like limestone, silica and gypsum. Coal and electric power are needed apart from rail transportation.

The first cement plant was set up in Chennai in 1904. After Independence the industry expanded. The industry has strategically located plants in Gujarat that have suitable access to the market in the Gulf countries.

Do it yourself

Where would it be economically viable to set up cement manufacturing units? Find out where the plants are located in other states of India and find their names.

Teacher explanation

Why the chemical industry is widely spread: its raw materials are widely available, the products are used in almost every other industry and in agriculture, and the industry is its own largest consumer — so units locate near markets and refineries rather than near a single ore body.

Automobile and IT/Electronics Industries

Automobile industry

Automobiles provide vehicles for quick transport of goods, services and passengers. Trucks, buses, cars, motorcycles, scooters, three-wheelers and multi-utility vehicles are manufactured in India at various centres. After liberalisation, the coming in of new and contemporary models stimulated the demand for vehicles in the market, which led to the healthy growth of the industry, including passenger cars, two- and three-wheelers.

The industry is located around Delhi, Gurugram, Mumbai, Pune, Chennai, Kolkata, Lucknow, Indore, Hyderabad, Jamshedpur and Bengaluru.

Information technology and electronics industry

The electronics industry covers a wide range of products from transistor sets to television, telephones, cellular telecom, telephone exchange, radars, computers and many other equipment required by the telecommunication industry. Bengaluru has emerged as the electronic capital of India. Other important centres for electronic goods are Mumbai, Delhi, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai, Kolkata, Lucknow and Coimbatore. The major industry concentration is at Bengaluru, Noida, Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad and Pune.

A major impact of this industry has been on employment generation. The continuing growth in hardware and software is the key to the success of the IT industry in India.

Industrial Pollution and Environmental Degradation

Although industries contribute significantly to India’s economic growth and development, the increase in pollution of land, water, air and noise, and the resulting degradation of environment that they have caused, cannot be overlooked. Industries are responsible for four types of pollution: (a) air (b) water (c) land (d) noise. The polluting industries also include thermal power plants.

Air pollution

Air pollution is caused by the presence of a high proportion of undesirable gases, such as sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide. Air-borne particulate materials contain both solid and liquid particles like dust, sprays, mist and smoke. Smoke is emitted by chemical and paper factories, brick kilns, refineries and smelting plants, and by the burning of fossil fuels in big and small factories that ignore pollution norms. Toxic gas leaks can be very hazardous, with long-term effects — the Bhopal gas tragedy is the example the chapter asks you to recall. Air pollution adversely affects human health, animals, plants, buildings and the atmosphere as a whole.

Water pollution

Water pollution is caused by organic and inorganic industrial wastes and effluents discharged into rivers. The main culprits are paper, pulp, chemical, textile and dyeing, petroleum refineries, tanneries and electroplating industries, which let out dyes, detergents, acids, salts and heavy metals like lead and mercury, pesticides, fertilisers, synthetic chemicals with carbon, plastics and rubber into water bodies. Fly ash, phospho-gypsum and iron and steel slags are the major solid wastes in India.

Thermal pollution of water occurs when hot water from factories and thermal plants is drained into rivers and ponds before cooling. Wastes from nuclear power plants and nuclear and weapon production facilities cause cancers, birth defects and miscarriages.

Land pollution

Soil and water pollution are closely related. Dumping of wastes, especially glass, harmful chemicals, industrial effluents, packaging, salts and garbage, renders the soil useless. Rain water percolates to the soil carrying the pollutants to the ground, and the groundwater also gets contaminated.

Noise pollution

Noise pollution not only results in irritation and anger, it can also cause hearing impairment, increased heart rate and blood pressure among other physiological effects. Unwanted sound is an irritant and a source of stress. Industrial and construction activities, machinery, factory equipment, generators, saws and pneumatic and electric drills also make a lot of noise.

Control of Environmental Degradation

Every litre of waste water discharged by our industry pollutes eight times the quantity of freshwater. How can industrial pollution of fresh water be reduced? Some suggestions are:

  1. Minimising the use of water for processing by reusing and recycling it in two or more successive stages.
  2. Harvesting of rainwater to meet water requirements.
  3. Treating hot water and effluents before releasing them into rivers and ponds.

Treatment of industrial effluents can be done in three phases:

Three phases of effluent treatment
PhaseMethodWhat it involves
PrimaryMechanical meansScreening, grinding, flocculation and sedimentation
SecondaryBiological processBiological treatment of the effluent
TertiaryBiological, chemical and physical processesIncludes recycling of wastewater

Overdrawing of groundwater reserves by industry, where there is a threat to groundwater resources, also needs to be regulated legally.

Particulate matter in the air can be reduced by fitting smoke stacks to factories with electrostatic precipitators, fabric filters, scrubbers and inertial separators. Smoke can be reduced by using oil or gas instead of coal in factories.

Noise can be reduced by using machinery and equipment with silencers; generators should be fitted with silencers. Almost all machinery can be redesigned to increase energy efficiency and reduce noise. Noise-absorbing material may be used, apart from personal use of earplugs and earphones.

The challenge of sustainable development requires integration of economic development with environmental concerns.

NTPC shows the way

NTPC is a major power-providing corporation in India. It has ISO certification for EMS (Environment Management System) 14001. The corporation has a proactive approach for preserving the natural environment and resources like water, oil and gas, and fuels in places where it is setting up power plants. This has been possible through:

  • Optimum utilisation of equipment adopting latest techniques and upgrading existing equipment.
  • Minimising waste generation by maximising ash utilisation.
  • Providing green belts for nurturing ecological balance and addressing the question of special purpose vehicles for afforestation.
  • Reducing environmental pollution through ash pond management, ash water recycling system and liquid waste management.
  • Ecological monitoring, reviews and on-line database management for all its power stations.

Key Terms and Definitions

Flashcards

All key terms

Key terms and definitions
TermSimple explanation
ManufacturingProduction of goods in large quantities after processing from raw materials to more valuable products; it belongs to the secondary sector.
Secondary activityActivity in which primary materials are manufactured into finished goods — steel, cars, textiles, bakeries.
Agro-based industryAn industry that draws its raw material from agriculture — cotton, woollen, jute and silk textiles, rubber, sugar, tea, coffee, edible oil.
Mineral-based industryAn industry that uses minerals and metals as raw materials — iron and steel, cement, aluminium, machine tools, petrochemicals.
Basic or key industryAn industry that supplies its products as raw material to manufacture other goods — iron and steel, copper smelting, aluminium smelting.
Consumer industryAn industry that produces goods for direct use by consumers — sugar, toothpaste, paper, sewing machines, fans.
Small scale industryAn industry defined with reference to the maximum investment allowed on the assets of a unit — at present rupees one crore.
Public sector industryAn industry owned and operated by government agencies — BHEL, SAIL.
Private sector industryAn industry owned and operated by individuals or a group of individuals — TISCO, Bajaj Auto Ltd., Dabur Industries.
Joint sector industryAn industry jointly run by the state and individuals or a group of individuals — Oil India Ltd.
Cooperative sector industryAn industry owned and operated by producers or suppliers of raw materials, or workers, or both, who pool resources and share profits or losses proportionately — sugar in Maharashtra, coir in Kerala.
Heavy industryAn industry using heavy and bulky raw materials and producing heavy goods — iron and steel.
Light industryAn industry using light raw materials and producing light goods — electrical goods.
Value chainThe full sequence from raw material to the highest value added product; the textile industry is the only one in India complete in the value chain.
KhadiHandspun and handwoven cloth; a cottage industry providing large-scale employment to weavers at home.
Sericulture linkSilk textiles depend on the rearing of silkworms — one of the four major fibre crops of India.
Basic industryThe iron and steel industry, because all other industries — heavy, medium and light — depend on it for their machinery.
Nodal location factors for steelLow cost of iron ore, high grade raw materials in proximity, cheap labour and vast growth potential in the home market — which is why the Chhotanagpur plateau has the maximum concentration.
SmeltingExtracting a metal from its ore by heating — as in aluminium smelting, where bauxite is converted to alumina and then to aluminium.
DAPDi-ammonium phosphate, a phosphatic fertiliser; complex fertilisers combine nitrogen (N), phosphate (P) and potash (K).
Thermal pollution of waterPollution caused when hot water from factories and thermal plants is drained into rivers and ponds before cooling.
Fly ashA major solid waste of India, along with phospho-gypsum and iron and steel slags.
Effluent treatmentThree-phase treatment of industrial waste water — primary (mechanical), secondary (biological) and tertiary (biological, chemical and physical, including recycling).
Electrostatic precipitatorA device fitted to smoke stacks to reduce particulate matter in the air, along with fabric filters, scrubbers and inertial separators.
EMS 14001ISO certification for an Environment Management System, held by NTPC.

07

NCERT In-text Questions and Answers

The questions printed inside the chapter

These are the “Can you…” and activity questions that appear inside the chapter text. Model answers are based on the chapter itself.

1.

Do you have some ideas about these industries? (from the Diwali story)

Model answer

Yes — industries differ by size and organisation. Shoes, clothes and sugar are made by machines in large industries; some utensils are made in small industries; and diyas are made by individual artisans in household industry. This is the basis of classification by capital investment and by ownership.

2.

List the various manufactured products you use in your daily life and classify them.

Model answer

Transistors, electric bulbs, vegetable oil, cement, glassware, petrol, matches, scooters, automobiles, medicines. They can be grouped as agro-based (vegetable oil), mineral-based (cement, petrol), consumer goods (bulbs, medicines), basic goods (cement, petrol), heavy (automobiles) and light (bulbs, matches).

3.

Classify the following on the basis of bulk and weight of raw material and finished goods: oil, knitting needles, brassware, fuse wires, watches, sewing machines, shipbuilding, electric bulbs, paint brushes, automobiles.

Model answer

Heavy industries: oil, shipbuilding, automobiles, sewing machines, brassware. Light industries: knitting needles, fuse wires, watches, electric bulbs, paint brushes.

4.

Why did Mahatma Gandhi lay emphasis on spinning yarn and weaving khadi?

Model answer

Because khadi is handspun and handwoven and provides large-scale employment to weavers in their homes as a cottage industry. It keeps value addition and income in the village, reduces dependence on mill-made cloth, and supports self-reliance — the same principle that made the textile industry the only one complete in the value chain.

5.

Why is it important for our country to keep the mill sector loomage lower than power loom and handloom?

Model answer

Because handloom and powerloom weaving provide employment to a very large number of people and allow traditional skills and designs in cotton, silk, zari and embroidery to survive. Mills produce large quantities, but concentrating weaving in mills would reduce decentralised employment; hence weaving is kept highly decentralised.

6.

Can you explain why the sugar industry is ideally suited to the cooperative sector?

Model answer

Because it is seasonal and its raw material, sugarcane, is bulky and loses sucrose content in haulage. Farmers must crush cane quickly, so they pool resources in a cooperative, own the mill together, and share profits or losses proportionately — the same logic as the coir industry in Kerala.

7.

Where would it be economically viable to set up cement manufacturing units? Find out where the plants are located in other states and their names.

Model answer

Near sources of bulky raw materials — limestone, silica and gypsum — with coal, electric power and rail transport available, and close to construction markets. Plants are located in Gujarat (for the Gulf market), Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Chhattisgarh and Uttar Pradesh. (Plant names vary; the chapter names Chennai as the site of the first plant, 1904.)

8.

Make a list of all such goods made of steel that you can think of.

Model answer

Machinery and machine tools, rails and railway wagons, ships, automobiles and their bodies, bridges, buildings and reinforcement bars, pipes, utensils, cutlery, surgical instruments, telephonic and scientific equipment, defence equipment, tins and containers, and electrical appliances.

9.

Are these factories following environmental norms? (project work)

Model answer

To answer, visit one agro-based and one mineral-based industry and check: whether smoke stacks have precipitators or scrubbers; whether effluent is treated in the three phases before discharge; whether hot water is cooled first; whether noise is controlled with silencers and absorbing material; and whether groundwater use is metered. (Student answers will vary.)

08

NCERT Exercise Questions and Answers

End-of-chapter exercises, projects and activities

NCERT Exercises

Reproduced from the exercise section of the chapter, with model answers. Word limits are the ones the textbook sets.

1.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — Which one of the following industries uses bauxite as a raw material? (a) Aluminium smelting (b) Cement (c) Paper (d) Steel

Model answer

(a) Aluminium smelting. Alumina, and later aluminium, is obtained from bauxite, a clay-like substance.

2.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — Which one of the following industries manufactures telephones, computers, etc.? (a) Steel (b) Electronic (c) Aluminium smelting (d) Information technology

Model answer

(b) Electronic. The electronics industry covers products from transistor sets to television, telephones, cellular telecom, telephone exchange, radars and computers.

3.
NCERT exercise2 marks

What is manufacturing? (about 30 words)

Model answer

Manufacturing is the production of goods in large quantities after processing raw materials into more valuable products — for example paper from wood, sugar from sugarcane, iron and steel from iron ore and aluminium from bauxite. It belongs to the secondary sector.

4.
NCERT exercise2 marks

What are basic industries? Give an example. (about 30 words)

Model answer

Basic or key industries are those which supply their products as raw materials to manufacture other goods. Example: iron and steel, which all other industries — heavy, medium and light — depend on for their machinery. Copper and aluminium smelting are also basic industries.

5.
NCERT exercise5 marks

How do industries pollute the environment? (about 120 words)

Model answer

Industries cause four kinds of pollution. Air pollution comes from a high proportion of undesirable gases such as sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide, and from particulate matter — dust, sprays, mist and smoke — emitted by chemical and paper factories, brick kilns, refineries and smelting plants; toxic gas leaks can be very hazardous. Water pollution is caused by organic and inorganic wastes and effluents discharged into rivers by paper, pulp, chemical, textile and dyeing, petroleum refinery, tannery and electroplating industries, letting out dyes, detergents, acids, salts, heavy metals like lead and mercury, pesticides and fertilisers; fly ash, phospho-gypsum and iron and steel slags are the major solid wastes. Hot water drained before cooling causes thermal pollution, and nuclear wastes cause cancers and birth defects. Land pollution follows from dumping glass, chemicals, effluents, packaging, salts and garbage, which renders soil useless and contaminates groundwater. Noise pollution from machinery, generators, saws and drills causes irritation, hearing impairment, increased heart rate and blood pressure.

6.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Discuss the steps to be taken to minimise environmental degradation by industry. (about 120 words)

Model answer

Every litre of industrial waste water pollutes eight times the quantity of freshwater, so water use must be minimised by reusing and recycling it in two or more successive stages, and rainwater should be harvested to meet requirements. Hot water and effluents must be treated before release, in three phases: primary by mechanical means (screening, grinding, flocculation and sedimentation), secondary by biological process, and tertiary by biological, chemical and physical processes including recycling of wastewater. Overdrawing of groundwater by industry needs legal regulation. Particulate matter in air can be reduced by fitting smoke stacks with electrostatic precipitators, fabric filters, scrubbers and inertial separators, and smoke by using oil or gas instead of coal. Noise can be reduced by silencers on machinery and generators, redesigning machinery for energy efficiency, using noise-absorbing material and earplugs. NTPC’s EMS 14001 approach — optimum equipment utilisation, minimising waste, green belts, ash pond management and ecological monitoring — shows the way.

7.
NCERT activityActivity

Activity — Give one word for each of the following with regard to industry. (i) Used to drive machinery (5) P… (ii) People who work in a factory (6) W… (iii) Where the product is sold (6) M… (iv) A person who sells goods (8) R… (v) Thing produced (7) P… (vi) To make or produce (11) M… (vii) Land, water and air degraded (9) P…

Model answer

(i) POWER (ii) WORKER (iii) MARKET (iv) RETAILER (v) PRODUCT (vi) MANUFACTURE (vii) POLLUTION.

8.
NCERT activityActivity

Activity (word search) — (1) Textiles, sugar, vegetable oil and plantation industries deriving raw materials from agriculture are called… (2) The basic raw material for the sugar industry. (3) This fibre is also known as the “Golden Fibre”. (4) Iron ore, coking coal and limestone are the chief raw materials of this industry. (5) A public sector steel plant located in Chhattisgarh. (6) Railway diesel engines are manufactured in Uttar Pradesh at this place.

Model answer

(1) AGRO-BASED (2) SUGARCANE (3) JUTE (4) IRON AND STEEL (5) BHILAI (6) VARANASI (Diesel Locomotive Works).

09

Important Questions and Answers

Board-style practice

Practice questions

Written in the style of CBSE board papers. They are additional practice, not NCERT originals.

1.

Why is the manufacturing sector called the backbone of development? (5 marks)

Model answer

Because manufacturing industries help modernise agriculture, which forms the backbone of our economy, and reduce the heavy dependence of people on agricultural income by providing jobs in secondary and tertiary sectors. Industrial development is a precondition for the eradication of unemployment and poverty, which was the philosophy behind public sector industries and joint sector ventures, and it aims at bringing down regional disparities by establishing industries in tribal and backward areas. Export of manufactured goods expands trade and commerce and brings in much needed foreign exchange, and countries that transform raw materials into a wide variety of finished goods of higher value are prosperous. Hence the economic strength of a country is measured by the development of manufacturing industries.

2.

“Agriculture and industry move hand in hand.” Explain. (3 marks)

Model answer

Agro-industries have given a major boost to agriculture by raising its productivity. They depend on agriculture for raw materials and sell their products — irrigation pumps, fertilisers, insecticides, pesticides, plastic and PVC pipes, machines and tools — to farmers. Thus the development and competitiveness of manufacturing has assisted agriculturists in increasing production and made production processes efficient.

3.

Classify industries on the basis of ownership with examples. (4 marks)

Model answer

Public sector — owned and operated by government agencies, e.g. BHEL, SAIL. Private sector — owned and operated by individuals or a group of individuals, e.g. TISCO, Bajaj Auto Ltd., Dabur Industries. Joint sector — jointly run by the state and individuals or a group of individuals, e.g. Oil India Ltd. Cooperative sector — owned and operated by producers or suppliers of raw materials, workers or both, who pool resources and share profits or losses proportionately, e.g. the sugar industry in Maharashtra and the coir industry in Kerala.

4.

Describe the cotton textile industry of India. (5 marks)

Model answer

In ancient India cotton textiles were produced with hand spinning and handloom weaving; after the 18th century power-looms came into use, and the traditional industry suffered a setback during the colonial period because it could not compete with mill-made cloth from England. The first successful textile mill was established in Mumbai in 1854, and the two World Wars boosted demand from the United Kingdom. The industry was concentrated in the cotton growing belt of Maharashtra and Gujarat because of raw cotton, market, transport and accessible port facilities, labour and moist climate. It provides a living to farmers, cotton boll pluckers and workers in ginning, spinning, weaving, dyeing, designing, packaging, tailoring and sewing, and supports chemicals and dyes, packaging and engineering industries. Spinning is centralised in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu while weaving is highly decentralised; handspun khadi gives large-scale employment as a cottage industry. The industry is the only one self-reliant and complete in the value chain.

5.

Why are jute mills concentrated along the Hugli river? (3 marks)

Model answer

Because of proximity to the jute producing areas; inexpensive water transport supported by railways, roadways and waterways to move raw material to the mills; abundant water for processing raw jute; cheap labour from West Bengal and adjoining Bihar, Odisha and Uttar Pradesh; and Kolkata as a large urban centre providing banking, insurance and port facilities for export. India is the largest producer of raw jute and jute goods and the second exporter after Bangladesh.

6.

Why are sugar mills shifting to Maharashtra and the south? (3 marks)

Model answer

Because the cane produced there has a higher sucrose content, the cooler climate ensures a longer crushing season, and cooperatives are more successful in these states. Earlier, sixty per cent of mills were in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

7.

Why is the iron and steel industry called a basic and heavy industry? (3 marks)

Model answer

It is a basic industry because all other industries — heavy, medium and light — depend on it for their machinery, and steel is needed for engineering goods, construction material, defence, medical, telephonic and scientific equipment and consumer goods. It is a heavy industry because all the raw materials as well as the finished goods are heavy and bulky, entailing heavy transportation costs; iron ore, coking coal and limestone are needed in the ratio of about 4:2:1, with some manganese to harden the steel.

8.

Why is the Chhotanagpur plateau the leading iron and steel region? (2 marks)

Model answer

Because of its relative advantages — low cost of iron ore, high grade raw materials in proximity, cheap labour and vast growth potential in the home market.

9.

Why are aluminium smelting plants located where they are? (3 marks)

Model answer

Because bauxite, the raw material, is very bulky, and smelting needs a regular supply of electricity and an assured source of raw material at minimum cost — the two prime factors for the location of the industry. Plants are in Odisha, West Bengal, Kerala, Uttar Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu.

10.

What is the main problem of the fertiliser industry in India? (2 marks)

Model answer

That potash is entirely imported, because the country does not have any reserves of commercially usable potash or potassium compounds in any form. Nitrogenous (urea), phosphatic and complex fertilisers (N, P, K) are produced in India.

11.

Explain the four types of industrial pollution. (5 marks)

Model answer

Air: high proportions of undesirable gases such as sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide, and airborne particulate matter — dust, sprays, mist and smoke — from chemical and paper factories, brick kilns, refineries and smelting plants and the burning of fossil fuels; toxic gas leaks are very hazardous. Water: organic and inorganic industrial wastes and effluents discharged into rivers by paper, pulp, chemical, textile and dyeing, petroleum refinery, tannery and electroplating industries; fly ash, phospho-gypsum and iron and steel slags are major solid wastes; hot water causes thermal pollution; nuclear wastes cause cancers, birth defects and miscarriages. Land: dumping of glass, chemicals, effluents, packaging, salts and garbage renders soil useless and, as rain percolates, contaminates groundwater. Noise: industrial and construction activity, machinery, generators, saws and pneumatic and electric drills cause irritation, anger, hearing impairment, increased heart rate and blood pressure.

12.

What are the three phases of effluent treatment? (3 marks)

Model answer

Primary — mechanical means, involving screening, grinding, flocculation and sedimentation. Secondary — biological process. Tertiary — biological, chemical and physical processes, involving recycling of wastewater.

13.

How has NTPC tried to preserve the environment? (5 marks)

Model answer

NTPC, a major power-providing corporation, holds ISO certification for EMS (Environment Management System) 14001 and takes a proactive approach to preserving the natural environment and resources like water, oil and gas and fuels where it sets up power plants. This has been possible through optimum utilisation of equipment by adopting the latest techniques and upgrading existing equipment; minimising waste generation by maximising ash utilisation; providing green belts for nurturing ecological balance and addressing special purpose vehicles for afforestation; reducing environmental pollution through ash pond management, ash water recycling systems and liquid waste management; and ecological monitoring, reviews and on-line database management for all its power stations.

14.

Why must Indian industry be efficient and competitive today? (2 marks)

Model answer

Because in the present-day world of globalisation, self-sufficiency alone is not enough. Our manufactured goods must be at par in quality with those in the international market, only then can we compete.

Previous Year Questions (PYQs)

Asked in CBSE board exams

Previous year questions

These follow the pattern of questions set in CBSE Social Science papers for this chapter. Answers are model answers.

1.
CBSE pattern

Why is the textile industry the only industry in India which is self-reliant and complete in the value chain? (CBSE pattern, 2 marks)

Model answer

Because it covers everything from raw material — cotton, jute, silk, wool — to the highest value added products such as garments, and contributes significantly to industrial production, employment generation and foreign exchange earnings.

2.
CBSE pattern

Explain any three factors responsible for the localisation of the cotton textile industry in Maharashtra and Gujarat. (3 marks)

Model answer

Availability of raw cotton from the cotton growing belt, market, transport including accessible port facilities, labour, and moist climate.

3.
CBSE pattern

Which is the electronic capital of India? Name two other important centres. (2 marks)

Model answer

Bengaluru. Other important centres include Mumbai, Delhi, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai, Kolkata, Lucknow and Coimbatore; the major concentration is at Bengaluru, Noida, Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad and Pune.

4.
CBSE pattern

What is a small scale industry? What is the present investment limit? (2 marks)

Model answer

A small scale industry is defined with reference to the maximum investment allowed on the assets of a unit; at present the maximum investment allowed is rupees one crore. This limit has changed over time.

5.
CBSE pattern

Why is the cement industry located near limestone deposits? (2 marks)

Model answer

Because it requires bulky and heavy raw materials — limestone, silica and gypsum — along with coal, electric power and rail transportation, so transport cost makes location near the raw material essential.

6.
CBSE pattern

Name the joint sector industry given in the chapter. (1 mark)

Model answer

Oil India Ltd. (OIL), jointly owned by the public and private sector.

7.
CBSE pattern

How much water is polluted by one litre of industrial waste water? (1 mark)

Model answer

Eight times the quantity of freshwater.

8.
CBSE pattern

Mention any two devices fitted to smoke stacks to reduce particulate matter. (2 marks)

Model answer

Electrostatic precipitators and fabric filters; also scrubbers and inertial separators.

9.
CBSE pattern

Why did the traditional cotton textile industry suffer a setback during the colonial period? (2 marks)

Model answer

Because it could not compete with the mill-made cloth imported from England.

10.
CBSE pattern

Name the industry which is its own largest consumer. (1 mark)

Model answer

The chemical industry — basic chemicals undergo processing to produce other chemicals used in industry, agriculture or consumer markets.

11

Frequently Asked Questions

Quick clarifications

1.

Is manufacturing a primary or secondary activity?

Model answer

Secondary — it processes primary materials into finished goods.

2.

What is the difference between a basic industry and a consumer industry?

Model answer

A basic (key) industry supplies its products as raw material to manufacture other goods, such as iron and steel. A consumer industry produces goods for direct use by consumers, such as sugar, toothpaste, paper, sewing machines and fans.

3.

Why is iron and steel called a heavy industry?

Model answer

Because both the raw materials and the finished goods are heavy and bulky, entailing heavy transportation costs.

4.

What is meant by “value chain”?

Model answer

The full sequence from raw material to the highest value added product. The textile industry is the only Indian industry complete in the value chain.

5.

Why is potash imported?

Model answer

Because India has no reserves of commercially usable potash or potassium compounds in any form.

6.

Which city is called the electronic capital of India?

Model answer

Bengaluru.

7.

What is thermal pollution of water?

Model answer

Pollution caused when hot water from factories and thermal plants is drained into rivers and ponds before cooling.

8.

What does EMS 14001 mean?

Model answer

It is the ISO certification for an Environment Management System, which NTPC holds.

Assertion-Reason Questions

Choose the correct option

How to answer

(a) Both A and R are true and R explains A. (b) Both are true but R does not explain A. (c) A is true, R is false. (d) A is false, R is true.

1.

Assertion (A): Manufacturing is part of the secondary sector.
Reason (R): It processes primary materials into finished goods.

2.

Assertion (A): Manufacturing is called the backbone of development.
Reason (R): It modernises agriculture, creates jobs and earns foreign exchange.

3.

Assertion (A): Iron and steel is a basic industry.
Reason (R): All other industries depend on it for their machinery.

4.

Assertion (A): The sugar industry is suited to the cooperative sector.
Reason (R): It is seasonal in nature.

5.

Assertion (A): Jute mills are concentrated along the Hugli river.
Reason (R): The Hugli basin is close to jute producing areas and has inexpensive water transport.

6.

Assertion (A): Aluminium smelting plants are located near coalfields.
Reason (R): Aluminium smelting requires a regular supply of electricity.

7.

Assertion (A): India imports all its potash.
Reason (R): India has no commercially usable reserves of potash.

8.

Assertion (A): Industrial waste water is harmless.
Reason (R): Every litre of industrial waste water pollutes eight times the quantity of freshwater.

9.

Assertion (A): NTPC holds ISO certification for EMS 14001.
Reason (R): It minimises waste generation by maximising ash utilisation.

10.

Assertion (A): Noise pollution affects health.
Reason (R): It can cause hearing impairment, increased heart rate and blood pressure.

Source-Based and Case-Based Questions

Read the passage or table, then answer

Source 1 — The Diwali market

Case study

On the occasion of Diwali, Harish went to a market with his parents. They purchased shoes and clothes for him. His mother purchased utensils, sugar, tea and diyas (earthen lamps). Harish observed that the shops in the market were flooded with items for sale. He wondered how so many items could be made in such large quantities. His father explained that shoes, clothes, sugar etc. are manufactured by machines in large industries, some utensils are manufactured in small industries, while items like diyas are made by individual artisans in household industry.

1.

Which items in the passage come from large industries?

Model answer

Shoes, clothes and sugar — manufactured by machines in large industries.

2.

What decides whether an industry is large, small or household?

Model answer

The scale of operation and capital investment — the chapter defines a small scale industry by the maximum investment allowed on its assets, at present rupees one crore.

3.

Which type of industry makes diyas, and why is it important?

Model answer

Household industry, run by individual artisans. It provides livelihood and keeps traditional skills alive, as with khadi weaving as a cottage industry.

Source 2 — Data: location factors of the jute industry

Data interpretation
Factors for the location of jute mills in the Hugli basin
FactorAdvantage
ProximityClose to jute producing areas
TransportInexpensive water transport, plus railways, roadways and waterways
WaterAbundant water for processing raw jute
LabourCheap labour from West Bengal, Bihar, Odisha and Uttar Pradesh
Urban facilitiesKolkata provides banking, insurance and port facilities for export

How to read this table: each row is a location factor and the advantage it gives. Together they explain why the mills form a narrow belt along one river.

1.

Which two factors relate to moving material rather than to labour?

Model answer

Proximity to jute producing areas and inexpensive transport by water, rail, road and waterway.

2.

Why is abundant water needed in this industry?

Model answer

For processing raw jute.

3.

Which single city provides several of these advantages at once?

Model answer

Kolkata — a large urban centre with banking, insurance and port facilities for export.

Source 3 — NTPC and environmental management

Case study

NTPC is a major power-providing corporation in India. It has ISO certification for EMS (Environment Management System) 14001. The corporation has a proactive approach for preserving the natural environment and resources like water, oil and gas and fuels in places where it is setting up power plants. This has been possible through optimum utilisation of equipment adopting latest techniques and upgrading existing equipment; minimising waste generation by maximising ash utilisation; providing green belts for nurturing ecological balance and addressing the question of special purpose vehicles for afforestation; reducing environmental pollution through ash pond management, ash water recycling system and liquid waste management; and ecological monitoring, reviews and on-line database management for all its power stations.

1.

What certification does NTPC hold and what does it cover?

Model answer

ISO certification for EMS 14001 — an Environment Management System.

2.

Name three ways in which NTPC reduces environmental pollution.

Model answer

Maximising ash utilisation to minimise waste; ash pond management, ash water recycling and liquid waste management; and green belts for ecological balance.

3.

Why is a thermal power corporation’s environmental record especially important?

Model answer

Because thermal power stations burn non-renewable fossil fuels and are named among polluting industries; they emit smoke and particulate matter and use large quantities of water, so good practice here prevents a great deal of pollution.

HOTS and Competency-Based Questions

Think beyond the text

Higher order thinking

These ask you to apply, compare or evaluate. Model answers are indicative — your own well-reasoned answer can differ.

1.

A company wants to set up a new steel plant. Using this chapter, list the factors it must weigh and where in India it would look.

Model answer

It needs iron ore, coking coal and limestone in about 4:2:1 ratio plus manganese, all heavy and bulky, so transport cost dominates; it also needs cheap labour, an efficient transport network for finished products, and a large home market. The Chhotanagpur plateau offers low cost iron ore, high grade raw materials in proximity, cheap labour and vast growth potential. If it locates elsewhere, it must justify the extra freight by market access or port facilities. (Model answer.)

2.

Why does India export raw jute but import jute goods from Bangladesh, even though it is the largest producer of raw jute? What should change?

Model answer

The chapter notes that India is the largest producer of raw jute and jute goods but stands second as an exporter after Bangladesh, and that after Partition the mills stayed in India while three-fourths of the jute area went to Bangladesh — so the two countries’ industries are interlinked. To gain more value, India must add value at home: modernise mills, diversify jute products (not only gunny bags but geo-textiles and composites), keep the mill belt competitive on power and labour costs, and brand jute as an eco-friendly fibre. (Model answer.)

3.

“Every litre of waste water pollutes eight times the quantity of freshwater.” Explain what this means for a riverside town with three textile dyeing units.

Model answer

It means the pollution load multiplies: a small discharge damages a much larger volume of clean water, so the town’s river and groundwater can be spoiled by relatively little effluent. The units must therefore minimise water use by reusing and recycling it, harvest rainwater to reduce drawdown, treat effluents in three phases before release, and cool hot water first. The town should also monitor and legally regulate groundwater overdrawal and enforce norms. (Model answer.)

4.

Compare a public sector steel plant with a cooperative sugar mill in terms of ownership, purpose and risk.

Model answer

A public sector plant such as SAIL or BHEL is owned and operated by government agencies, aims at national development, employment and reducing regional disparities, and bears risk through the exchequer. A cooperative sugar mill is owned by producers who pool resources and share profits or losses proportionately; it exists to get members’ cane crushed quickly, since the bulky raw material loses sucrose in haulage, and being seasonal it suits cooperative ownership. Both are alternatives to purely private enterprise. (Model answer.)

5.

Bengaluru has neither iron ore nor coal, yet it is India’s electronic capital. Explain this using the chapter’s ideas of location.

Model answer

Because the electronics and IT industry is not raw-material based: its inputs are skilled people, electricity, connectivity and markets. Its products are light and of high value, so transport cost hardly matters, and it benefits from agglomeration — firms, institutes and talent clustering together. This shows that the location logic of light, knowledge-based industry differs completely from that of heavy industry, which must sit near bulky raw materials. (Model answer.)

6.

Design three practical rules a school could adopt to reduce the pollution footprint of a nearby factory it buys uniforms from.

Model answer

(i) Ask for evidence that dyeing effluent is treated in three phases before discharge and that hot water is cooled first. (ii) Require that the factory’s smoke stacks have electrostatic precipitators or scrubbers and that it uses oil or gas rather than coal. (iii) Insist on noise control — silencers on generators, noise-absorbing material — and on rainwater harvesting and water recycling, with an annual report. (Model answer.)

Quick Revision Sheet

One page before the exam

Basics

  • Manufacturing = processing raw materials into more valuable products; secondary sector.
  • Economic strength measured by manufacturing; backbone of development (4 reasons).
  • Agriculture and industry move hand in hand; globalisation demands quality.

Classification

  • Raw material: agro-based, mineral-based.
  • Role: basic/key, consumer.
  • Capital: small scale (max rupees one crore).
  • Ownership: public (BHEL, SAIL), private (TISCO, Bajaj, Dabur), joint (OIL), cooperative (sugar Maharashtra, coir Kerala).
  • Bulk: heavy (iron and steel), light (electrical goods).

Textiles

  • Only industry complete in the value chain.
  • First mill Mumbai 1854; power-looms after 18th century; colonial setback.
  • Maharashtra and Gujarat: raw cotton, market, transport, ports, labour, moist climate.
  • Spinning centralised (Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu); weaving decentralised; khadi.

Jute and sugar

  • Jute: largest producer of raw jute and goods; second exporter after Bangladesh; Hugli belt; first mill Rishra 1855; Partition 1947.
  • Sugar: second in sugar, first in gur and khandsari; 60% mills UP and Bihar; seasonal → cooperative; shift south/west for sucrose, cooler climate, cooperatives.

Mineral-based

  • Iron and steel: basic + heavy; 4:2:1; Chhotanagpur plateau; index of development.
  • Aluminium: second metallurgical industry; 4–6 t bauxite → 2 t alumina → 1 t aluminium; electricity and raw material decide location.
  • Chemicals: inorganic (sulphuric acid, soda ash, caustic soda), organic (petrochemicals); own largest consumer.
  • Fertiliser: N, P, K; potash imported; Gujarat, TN, UP, Punjab, Kerala = half.
  • Cement: limestone, silica, gypsum; first plant Chennai 1904; Gujarat for Gulf market.
  • Automobile: Delhi, Gurugram, Mumbai, Pune, Chennai, Kolkata, Lucknow, Indore, Hyderabad, Jamshedpur, Bengaluru.
  • IT/electronics: Bengaluru electronic capital; employment generation.

Pollution and control

  • Four types: air, water, land, noise; thermal plants included.
  • Air: SO2, CO, particulates; Bhopal gas tragedy.
  • Water: effluents; fly ash, phospho-gypsum, steel slag; thermal pollution; nuclear waste.
  • Control: reuse and recycle water, rainwater harvesting, three-phase treatment, regulate groundwater, precipitators/fabric filters/scrubbers/inertial separators, oil or gas instead of coal, silencers, redesign, earplugs.
  • NTPC: EMS 14001; equipment, ash utilisation, green belts, ash pond management, ecological monitoring.

Chapter Summary

The whole chapter in a few paragraphs

Manufacturing — the production of goods in large quantities after processing raw materials into more valuable products — belongs to the secondary sector, and the economic strength of a country is measured by the development of its manufacturing industries. Manufacturing modernises agriculture, reduces dependence on agricultural income, is a precondition for eradicating unemployment and poverty, brings down regional disparities and expands trade, earning foreign exchange. Agriculture and industry move hand in hand, and in a globalising world Indian goods must match international quality.

Industries are classified by source of raw material (agro-based and mineral-based), main role (basic and consumer), capital investment (small scale, with a limit of rupees one crore on assets), ownership (public, private, joint and cooperative) and bulk and weight (heavy and light). The cotton textile industry — the only one complete in the value chain — grew from hand spinning to power-looms, with the first mill in Mumbai in 1854, and is concentrated in Maharashtra and Gujarat. Jute mills form a narrow belt along the Hugli, with the first mill at Rishra in 1855, and India is the largest producer of raw jute and jute goods. Sugar, second in the world but first in gur and khandsari, is seasonal and suited to cooperatives, and is shifting south and west.

Among mineral-based industries, iron and steel is both basic and heavy, needs iron ore, coking coal and limestone in about 4:2:1, and is concentrated on the Chhotanagpur plateau. Aluminium smelting is the second most important metallurgical industry; the chemical industry is its own largest consumer; potash for fertiliser is entirely imported; the first cement plant was set up in Chennai in 1904; automobiles cluster around Delhi, Mumbai, Pune, Chennai, Kolkata, Lucknow, Indore, Hyderabad, Jamshedpur and Bengaluru; and Bengaluru is the electronic capital.

Industries pollute air, water, land and noise. Control requires minimising and recycling water, rainwater harvesting, three-phase effluent treatment, legal regulation of groundwater, precipitators, fabric filters, scrubbers and inertial separators, oil or gas instead of coal, and silencers and noise-absorbing material. NTPC, with ISO certification for EMS 14001, shows how a power corporation can integrate economic development with environmental concerns.
